paragraphs.text: Cole-Carpenter syndrome-2 is a rare skeletal dysplasia associated with low bone mass or an osteogenesis imperfecta-like phenotype (Takeyari et al., 2018). Its features include severely disturbed ossification of the skull and multiple fractures beginning before birth. Patients also have short stature and craniofacial malformations, including macrocephaly, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, and micrognathia (Garbes et al., 2015).

In their report, one patient most closely resembled Cole-Carpenter syndrome and 2 fetuses were initially suspected to have a severe type of osteogenesis imperfecta. Moosa et al. paragraphs.text: Garbes et al. (2015) reported 3 affected individuals from 2 families with a similar skeletal phenotype. They were a 7-year-old boy whose phenotype most closely resembled Cole-Carpenter syndrome and 2 fetuses initially suspected to have a severe type of osteogenesis imperfecta. All 3 had severely disturbed ossification of the skull and multiple fractures with prenatal onset. The boy had short stature and craniofacial malformations, including macrocephaly, midface hypoplasia, micrognathia, frontal bossing, and downslanting palpebral fissures. The authors compared the disorder with cranio-lenticulo-sutural dysplasia (CLSD), which is caused by SEC23A mutations and has a largely overlapping craniofacial phenotype. However, CLSD is not characterized by generalized bone fragility, and the original family with CLSD had cataracts.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2017) studied 2 Chinese families with osteogenesis imperfecta. The proband in family 1 was a 23-year-old man with recurrent fractures, dentinogenesis imperfecta, an unclosed anterior fontanel, and facial dysmorphism. Three-dimensional CT imaging of his cranium showed skull deformities with a broad ossification defect in the frontoapical area, a widened sagittal suture, and wormian bones. The proband in family 2 was a 7-year-old boy who also had recurrent fractures, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and an unclosed anterior fontanel, but no obvious facial dysmorphism.

paragraphs.text: Using whole-exome sequencing, Garbes et al. (2015) identified 3 mutant SEC24D alleles in 3 affected individuals from 2 families. The alleles were a truncating mutation, c.613C-T (Q205X), and 2 missense mutations: c.3044C-T (S1015F), located in a cargo-binding pocket, and c.2933A-C (Q978P), located in the gelsolin-like domain. Each affected individual was compound heterozygous for 2 of these alleles. The c.3044C-T mutation lay within a 14-Mb founder haplotype shared by all 3. In skin fibroblasts from the affected boy, electron and immunofluorescence microscopy showed inefficient export of procollagen from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and dilated ER tubules. This reproduced the cellular phenotype of individuals with CLSD. The authors noted that the cellular and morphologic phenotypes were in concordance with those of the Sec24d-deficient fish mutants vbi (medaka) and bulldog (zebrafish).

paragraphs.text: Using whole-exome sequencing in a 15-year-old Japanese boy with Cole-Carpenter syndrome, Takeyari et al. (2018) identified compound heterozygous variants in the SEC24D gene: R313H and R484X.

checks.evidence_quote: Whole exome sequencing analysis identified biallelic variants in SEC24D (p.Arg484* and p.Arg313His) in the patient.

paragraphs.text: Using whole-exome sequencing in a 15-year-old Japanese boy with Cole-Carpenter syndrome, Takeyari et al. (2018) identified compound heterozygous variants in the SEC24D gene. One resulted in an arg484-to-ter (R484X) substitution, and the other was R313H. The patient had short-trunk short stature, ocular proptosis, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, micrognathia, low bone mineral density, and basilar impression.
